name: Loop 1: The founding questions
title: The founding questions
premise: The model specified obligations precisely and witnessed their breach almost nowhere. Requirements, verifications, exceptions, and communication policies were all stated with real precision, and in each case the execution-side counterpart that would catch a violation was missing. Loop 1 asks each of the twelve named roles what it actually needs to know, and invents the atomic predicates required to answer.

name: Loop 2: Questions only loop 1 made askable
title: Questions only loop 1 made askable
premise: Loop 1 established WHAT can go wrong: a blocking control unmet, a verification skipped, a send refused, a claim whose source has left. Loop 2 asks the questions that only exist once those columns do — about the QUALITY of the assurance rather than its presence. Three examples that had no expressible form before loop 1 ran: only 4 of 13 requirements have any computed witness at all, so which controls are still trusted purely on assertion; verification_outcomes.is_self_witnessed reads 3/4, so how much of the evidence is the executor vouching for themselves; and send_intents.is_silently_dropped reads 4/7, a failure mode that could not be named until IsClearedToSend existed to refuse a send in the first place. Every loop-2 question records, in its own provenance, the loop-1 predicates that made it possible.

name: Loop 3: Loop 3: the three gaps the source articles named and the model didn't have
title: Loop 3: the three gaps the source articles named and the model didn't have
premise: Comparing this rulebook against the four "Intentional Arrangement" Process Knowledge Management articles surfaced three concepts the essays argue for at length that had no table: process mining as an elicitation channel, controlled vocabulary/taxonomy, and the informal knowledge-broker network. Unlike loops 1-2, this loop is not a full 12-role sweep — it is exactly these three named gaps, each owned by the role that would actually ask the question.

name: Loop 4: Structure the executions cannot show
title: Structure the executions cannot show
premise: Every witness in loops 1-3 reads either a single row or a single edge: whether this transition was traversed, whether this control was satisfied. The step graph itself is cyclic (Fallback and Alternative transitions send work back to earlier steps), and questions about its shape (which steps can be re-entered, which controls must hold on every pass) are reachability over paths of any length. Transitive closure is provably not expressible in first-order logic with aggregates, so no formula answers them. Loop 4 adds the closure of StepTransitions as a substrate-native closure field and asks the questions only it makes askable.

name: Loop 6: Loop 6: the full PKO class model, lockout/tagout, and a governed deployment
title: Loop 6: the full PKO class model, lockout/tagout, and a governed deployment
premise: Loop 5 put every claim of the five source articles into the rulebook and computed what the model covers. The largest block of uncovered claims was structural: PKO 2.0.0 classes and properties with no table (multi-steps and their children, input and output variables, the entities an execution used and generated, status-change kinds, FAQ categories and targets, the industry module's machines, energy sources, locks and protective equipment), and the two worked procedures the articles tell their story through. This loop adds both, and every new predicate is asked for by the technician, safety officer, steward or knowledge engineer doing that work.

name: Loop 7: Loop 7: elicitation methods and tacit knowledge
title: Loop 7: elicitation methods and tacit knowledge
premise: Loop 6 gave the model a lockout/tagout procedure encoded from veterans' workshops, with the executions that show where practice departs from the SOP. What the model still could not say was how that knowledge was drawn out: which methods were combined, whether interviews asked why and what happens when the procedure falls short, what observation saw that the practitioner never mentioned, who was in the workshop, which disagreements were settled, what an expert knows but cannot say, where the knowledge lived before and after, and whether gatekept knowledge was ever drawn out. This loop adds each of those with seeded breaches.

name: Loop 8: Loop 8: organizing collected knowledge before modeling it
title: Loop 8: organizing collected knowledge before modeling it
premise: Loop 6 gave the model the full PKO class model and two worked procedures; loop 7 records how their knowledge was collected. Nothing yet says how that material is organized: at which level of abstraction a statement lives, which stakeholder lens a view serves, where a piece of knowledge applies and where it stops, how coarse a step is, which taxonomy branch a procedure sits in, which wording practitioners use for an activity or a role, and whether the controlled terms still mean what the organization means. This loop organizes it, and every predicate is asked for by the steward, knowledge engineer, auditor, product manager, infrastructure engineer, operations manager or executive who needs that organization to do their work.

name: Loop 9: Loop 9: encoded knowledge in use -- retrieval, AI grounding, projections and feedback
title: Loop 9: encoded knowledge in use -- retrieval, AI grounding, projections and feedback
premise: Loop 6 gave the model the lockout/tagout and production-deployment procedures, their executions and the AI risk classifier. Nothing yet recorded how that knowledge leaves the rulebook: which systems hold which version, what graph an AI assistant was served and whether a reasoner checked it, which segments and assertions grounded an answer, what prompts carried, which documents were generated from the model, what practitioners annotated, searched for and failed to find, and what outcomes followed. Those records only became judgeable once loop 6 made the steps, transitions, conditions, cues and requirements explicit enough to check an AI's output against. Every predicate here is asked for by the knowledge engineer, steward, safety officer, release manager, AI enablement lead or the plant assistant itself.

name: Loop 10: Loop 10: the model governs itself: ownership, versioning, change control and question review
title: Loop 10: the model governs itself: ownership, versioning, change control and question review
premise: Loops 6 to 9 gave the procedures their full structure, organization and encoding, and every one of those loops changed this rulebook's schema. Nothing recorded who was allowed to make those changes, which competency question motivated them, what their impact assessment found, which semantic version they shipped in, or whether the original questions still answer afterwards. This loop makes the model's own governance data: named steward and authority charters, a change log and change requests with impact findings and validation runs, releases whose version numbers are checked against their contents, drift observations, and a competency-question baseline re-run per release.

name: Loop 11: Loop 11: sourcing, knowledge audit, the AI system registry and ground-truth routing
title: Loop 11: sourcing, knowledge audit, the AI system registry and ground-truth routing
premise: Loop 6 gave the model a governed production deployment with an AI risk classifier, role assignments with validity periods, and the artifacts each step produces and consumes. What the model still could not say was where the organization's process knowledge actually lives once execution is sent to providers, what an audit of held against needed knowledge finds, whether provider relationships move knowledge back, which AI systems the registry knows that the graph does not, what an agent upgrade touches, and whether the assignments that a deployment pipeline routes approval notices from were updated before the run that needed them. This loop adds each of those, with seeded breaches on the deployment scenario.

name: Loop 12: Loop 12: the social side of collection: holders, brokers, communities, trust and turnover
title: Loop 12: the social side of collection: holders, brokers, communities, trust and turnover
premise: Loops 6 to 11 gave the model procedures, executions, role assignments with departures, a broker network, communities of practice and a sourcing audit. What the model still could not say was who carries each piece of know-how (a person, a facility or a system), how it travels, who bridges communities and translates their vocabularies, what a source withholds under which power dynamic, whether departments disagree about the same process, whether mentors have time and sharers are rewarded, and whether knowledge and solved problems survive staff turnover. This loop adds each of those, with seeded breaches on the lockout and deployment scenarios.

name: Loop 13: Loop 13: provenance, traceability, process mining and the document-practice gap
title: Loop 13: provenance, traceability, process mining and the document-practice gap
premise: Earlier loops recorded collected source material, elicitation sessions, knowledge fragments with a source agent, and process-mining runs as variant counts. What the model could not say was which collected material each process model, step and constraint came from and in what role, whether that source has changed since, who derived and who confirmed each item, where the mined flow departs from the documented one and where it waits, whether documents trail practice, and whether failures, feedback and recurring reviews actually flow back into collection. This loop adds each of those, with seeded breaches on the deployment and lockout scenarios.

name: Loop 14: Loop 14: use cases, experts, pilots and real data behind each governed model
title: Loop 14: use cases, experts, pilots and real data behind each governed model
premise: Loops 6 to 13 left a handful of article claims uncovered. Four are practices the Linked Open Terms methodology prescribes and theme E's governed models could not witness: starting from a real use case, domain experts in every activity, refinement through pilots, and implementation over real data.

name: Loop 15: The machinery around the knowledge: encoding technologies, funding programmes, published terms
title: The machinery around the knowledge: encoding technologies, funding programmes, published terms
premise: Loops 6 to 14 modelled ACME's procedural knowledge itself. Five article claims had no honest witness afterwards, because each is about the machinery around that knowledge rather than the knowledge: whether the systems holding it can query, validate and reason over it; whether the research programmes behind the ontologies it reuses are still running; whether its own extension terms are published so anyone can look them up; and which kinds of knowledge an abundance of information leaves wanting. Each became askable only once consumer systems, ontology profiles and the field catalog existed to point at.

name: Loop 16: Controlled is not the same as secured: who reads the register in full
title: Controlled is not the same as secured: who reads the register in full
premise: Loop 15's access-control seeding gave every governance table a policy, which silently retired the witness for 'access to process knowledge must be controlled': a column that asked whether a table had no policy at all now reads false everywhere. The question that only became askable once every table was policed is the sharper one -- of the policies that do exist, which ones cut no rows at all for a principal who is not an administrator. That condition is present in this model and an access review is exactly the exercise that looks for it.

name: Loop 17: What is read aloud must be on a page
title: What is read aloud must be on a page
premise: Loop 15 gave each role an app to work in, and rehearsing the video series in that app showed the difference between a fact the rows support and a fact a person can find. Seven sentences of narration were true and visible nowhere: totals by kind of knowledge, by who did an assistant's reasoning, by execution order and by mapping relation; the community a mentorship belongs to; and the path from a cancelled run to the gap it stopped at and the change that answers it. Those questions only became askable once people could sign in and look.
